313.history: The rock-hollow landing on the river took in the hewers of Muileann dhearg when their pits closed. The families walked down behind carts the guild found for them in the tenth year and lay the first winter in the Board's sheds by the landing, going into the new row as each house was roofed; the town calls it Sreath nan Gualadairean. Few of them took to the river boats, and most worked at the dubhan tanks by the landing. Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, the last master of Comann nan Gualadairean, came back to Seann Toll when the guild was dissolved and died there in {{year:VI-0040}}, and Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd entered his death herself. The river landing is also the landing of Còmhrag Ceann leathan crowds going down to Ceann leathan by boat, and in the fair weeks Sreath nan Gualadairean lets rooms to them; the row's children are counted in the town's roll as children of Seann Toll, and the older hewers still give Muileann dhearg as their town when asked.

491.history: The town of the red mill beside Cill ghlas lost its pits in {{year:VI-0032}}. The Board's surveyor wrote them spent, the last shift came up, and the youngest hewer stood with the last lamp used on the face until the pit captain hung it on the rack himself. The families walked down to Seann Toll. The druid house of the town was given to its caretaker to keep with the graves, and once a year Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean sends a teacher to give the one lecture that remains, to an empty quarter and few hearers. The red mill grinds on. The red mill beside Cill ghlas never belonged to the pits and grinds for the farms of the district as it did before the coal; the miller bought a dubhan engine for the dry summers and keeps the wheel for the wet ones. The pit-heads stand roofless on the hill above the town.
491.known_for: the pits that closed and the lecture given to an empty quarter

197.history: The great eastern river port and pilgrims' landing keeps Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, which in the fourth year disputed the Àrd-choimheadaiche's letter on the new fuel. In {{year:VI-0036}} a letter of the school's masters to the library first used the word dubhan-tùsail, of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise; they used it of their own school's revival, and the library entered it and has never used it. The school still sends a teacher once a year to Muileann dhearg. A river-boat with a dubhan engine has carried pilgrims up to the landing against the current since the ninth year, in half the time of the rowed boats.
197.known_for: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, and the word dubhan-tùsail

135.history: The deep-field town of the camps' granaries above An Sloc Mòr was the hewers' own. Comann nan Gualadairean kept its hall there and its day of binding, which passed empty in the first year with no son or daughter brought to be bound. The hall was sold before the guild was dissolved in {{year:VI-0038}}, and became a dubhan depot with its carved lintel, the guild's oath cut in it, left above the pumps; the oath-stone went to the library. Comhairle nam Mèinnean bought the last private share in An Sloc Mòr when Taigh Mhic Ùisdein moved to shipping, and its pumps ran on dubhan from the thirteenth year. In {{year:VI-0144}} An Sloc Mòr was closed, one face kept for Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, its upper galleries capped; twelve hewers were sworn at the town to cut the altar-coal, one an old man who had sworn the guild's oath in his youth, and in the present year the four baskets of their coal were carried south to the lot.
135.known_for: Comann nan Gualadairean' hall, An Sloc Mòr and the altar-coal

229.history: The small town of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh had Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house for their sick, and lost its coal before most. In the second year the keeper let the boilers go cold and found the springs warm enough alone. When the guild dissolved, the bath-house passed with its other goods to the custodians of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in {{year:VI-0039}}, who kept the old keeper and the same sick, hewers' widows first. A bus of Cathair dhearg ran to the springs twice weekly from the thirteenth year and filled the benches with townsfolk who were not sick. In the war the custodians took in two wounded officers of the regiments at the council's asking. In the wet summer of the twenty-fifth year the springs ran so full that the lower room flooded.
229.known_for: Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh and Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house given to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail

27.history: The capital country's great merchant port held the guild court of the shipwrights, which sat on the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich in {{year:VI-0013}}, and sold the launch engines that went into the first engine-boats. Taigh Mhic Ùisdein put its money into dubhan shipping here in the thirteenth year, the only house of the vein that moved before the vein failed it, and the first of its hulls took shape in the Ros dhomhain yards. The kingdom's patrol boats were refitted for dubhan here and outran the raiders; the eleven taken were tried in Cùirt na Mara, the eight Dia-thìrich sent to the quarries and the three Tuathaich sent north. In the present year the first tank-hull under Dubhan's Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt, An Eala Dhubh, was loaded at Ros dhomhain over three days, searched and sealed by the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde, and stood out on the morning tide with An t-Ionmhas's seal on her hatches.
27.known_for: Cùirt na Mara, Mac Ùisdein's hulls and the first export
